title: Local squared norm of an opposition-compatible root bracket
statement: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional semisimple $\mathbf Q$-Lie algebra [def-wf-lie-algebra], [def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra]. Let $\mathfrak h\subseteq\mathfrak g$ be a maximal abelian subalgebra acting diagonally over $\mathbf Q$, with root decomposition $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak h\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in R}\mathfrak g_\alpha$, where $R\subset\mathfrak h^\vee\setminus\{0\}$ is its reduced crystallographic root system and $\mathfrak g_\alpha=\{z:[h,z]=\alpha(h)z\text{ for every }h\in\mathfrak h\}$ is one-dimensional. For $\alpha\in R$, let $h_\alpha\in[\mathfrak g_\alpha,\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}]\subseteq\mathfrak h$ be the coroot with $\alpha(h_\alpha)=2$. Let $\theta$ be a $\mathbf Q$-linear Lie automorphism with $\theta^2=1$ and $\theta(h)=-h$ for $h\in\mathfrak h$, carrying $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ to $\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$. Let $\alpha,\beta\in R$ with $\gamma=\alpha+\beta\in R$, and let $u\in\mathfrak g_\alpha$, $v\in\mathfrak g_\beta$ satisfy $[u,-\theta(u)]=h_\alpha$ and $[v,-\theta(v)]=h_\beta$. Put $p=\max\{n\in\mathbf Z_{\geq0}:\beta-n\alpha\in R\}$ and $w=[u,v]$. Then $$[w,-\theta(w)]=(p+1)^2h_\gamma.$$ In particular $w\ne0$.

source.place: Section 23h, Theorem 23.71, printed pp.508--509: agent-stated conditional local, squared-norm formulation of the root-string calculation. Unlike existence of a Chevalley basis, this assertion takes only two already normalized root vectors as input.

proof.text: Reducedness and $\alpha+\beta\in R$ imply $\beta\ne\pm\alpha$, hence $\alpha,\beta$ are linearly independent. Indeed a proportional root is $\pm\alpha$, and either alternative makes the sum zero or $2\alpha$, neither a root. The root-coroot clause of [lem-sfb-split-semisimple-root-decomposition] packages the given families as a finite reduced crystallographic root pairing $P$ for evaluation $\mathfrak h^\vee\times\mathfrak h\to\mathbf Q$. Apply [lem-sfb-rational-killing-root-duality] and write $B,b,t_\rho,d_\rho$ for its forms, Killing-dual vectors and positive squared lengths. In particular $[x,y]=B(x,y)t_\rho$ for opposite root vectors and $t_\rho=(d_\rho/2)h_\rho$.

source.place: Section 23h, pp.503,508--509; agent expansion of the local root-string calculation.

proof.text: Let $q=\max\{n\geq0:\beta+n\alpha\in R\}$; $q\geq1$ since $\gamma$ is a root. Apply [lem-sfb-root-string-integer-interval] to $P,\alpha,\beta$: the roots on this line are exactly $\beta+k\alpha$ with $-p\leq k\leq q$. Apply [lem-sfb-root-string-endpoint-difference] to the same independent pair and put $m=\beta(h_\alpha)$; it gives $m=p-q$ in $\mathbf Q$. Finally [lem-sfb-root-string-adjacent-length-ratio] applied to the positive reflection-invariant $b$ and $\gamma=\alpha+\beta$ gives $q d_\gamma=(p+1)d_\beta$.

source.place: Appendix C, pp.621--622, rank-two diagrams; root-string endpoints as in Section 23h, pp.504--505.

proof.text: Set $f=-\theta(u)$, $E=\operatorname{ad}u$ and $F=\operatorname{ad}f$. The normalization $[u,f]=h_\alpha$ and Jacobi give $EF-FE=\operatorname{ad}h_\alpha$. Put $V_k=\mathfrak g_{\beta+k\alpha}$ for $-p\leq k\leq q$. Every $V_k$ is one-dimensional by the item and the interval from step 2. Jacobi shows that $E:V_k\to V_{k+1}$ and $F:V_k\to V_{k-1}$; they vanish across an endpoint since that weight is neither zero nor a root. On $V_k$, $\operatorname{ad}h_\alpha$ is the scalar $m+2k$. Choose a nonzero basis vector in each $V_k$ and for $-p\leq k<q$ write $E z_k=a_kz_{k+1}$ and $F z_{k+1}=b_{k+1}z_k$. Let $c_k=a_kb_{k+1}$ for $k<q$ and $c_q=0$. Then $FE|_{V_k}=c_k$; for $1\leq k\leq q$ one has $EF|_{V_k}=c_{k-1}$. Evaluating the commutator on these $z_k$ gives $c_{k-1}-c_k=m+2k$. Summing for $k=1,\ldots,q$ yields $c_0=q m+q(q+1)=q(p+1)$. Thus $FE(v)=q(p+1)v$. This calculation uses products of scalar matrix entries and does not assume either transition map is invertible.

source.place: Section 23h, pp.504--505, rank-one root-string action; agent scalar recurrence for the actual adjoint representation.

proof.text: Since $\theta$ is an automorphism and $f=-\theta(u)$, $-\theta(w)=[f,\theta(v)]=F(\theta(v))$. Invariance and symmetry of $B$ give $B([f,x],y)=-B(x,[f,y])$, by replacing $[x,f]$ with $-[f,x]$ in $B(x,[f,y])=B([x,f],y)$. Therefore, using step 3, $$B(w,-\theta(w))=B(Ev,F\theta(v))=-B(FEv,\theta(v))=q(p+1)B(v,-\theta(v)).$$ The normalization of $v$ and opposite-root duality give $h_\beta=B(v,-\theta(v))t_\beta=B(v,-\theta(v))(d_\beta/2)h_\beta$. Apply $\beta$, for which $\beta(h_\beta)=2$, to obtain $B(v,-\theta(v))=2/d_\beta$.

source.place: Section 23h, pp.508--509, opposition-compatible normalization; agent invariant-form calculation.

proof.text: Jacobi puts $w$ in $\mathfrak g_\gamma$ and the hypothesis on $\theta$ puts $-\theta(w)$ in $\mathfrak g_{-\gamma}$. Apply opposite-root duality once more and substitute the scalar from step 4: $$[w,-\theta(w)]=\frac{2q(p+1)}{d_\beta}t_\gamma=\frac{q(p+1)d_\gamma}{d_\beta}h_\gamma=(p+1)^2h_\gamma.$$ The last equality is $q d_\gamma=(p+1)d_\beta$ from step 2; division is valid since $d_\beta>0$. Since $\gamma(h_\gamma)=2$ and $p+1$ is a positive rational integer, the right side is nonzero. A zero $w$ would give a zero bracket, proving $w\ne0$.

source.place: Section 23h, Theorem 23.71, pp.508--509; agent assembly by root-length cancellation.
